faq.a: Rarely; most cavities persist unless treated with appropriate anti‑TB therapy.
faq.q: Can a TB cavity heal on its own?

faq.a: Not necessarily, but large or persistent cavities after treatment raise suspicion for resistance.
faq.q: Is a cavity a sign of drug resistance?

faq.a: Standard 4‑drug regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months, followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin.
faq.q: What is the best first line drug for TB with a cavity?

exam: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 35‑year‑old man with chronic cough, weight loss, and a 2 cm cavity in the right upper lobe? — TB cavity; confirm with sputum smear and GeneXpert.
A patient with a known TB cavity develops sudden haemoptysis. What is the immediate management step? — Secure airway, give oxygen, and arrange urgent bronchoscopy or CT angiography.
Why is a thin‑walled cavity on X‑ray not always clinically significant? — It may represent a healed lesion; clinical correlation and sputum testing are needed.
What is the significance of a cavity wall >4 mm on CT? — Indicates chronic disease and higher risk of relapse; may need longer therapy.
How does HIV infection alter the presentation of a TB cavity? — Cavities may be smaller, atypical, or absent; high index of suspicion is required.
Why is rifampicin avoided in a patient with a severe hepatic injury? — It is hepatotoxic; alternative regimens must be considered.
What laboratory test would you order to rule out drug resistance in a patient with a persistent cavity after 2 months of therapy? — GeneXpert MTB/RIF or line‑probe assay.
ai.title: Pulmonary Tubercular Cavity
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A cavitary lesion in the lung caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It forms when necrotic tissue is liquefied and expelled, leaving a gas‑filled space. Recognising it guides diagnosis, treatment and prognosis.

sections.p: Tubercular cavities are the classic radiological hallmark of re‑activation TB in the upper lobes. They arise when caseous necrosis liquefies and is expelled through the bronchial tree, leaving a gas‑filled space surrounded by fibrous scar.

t.b: Shows a round or oval lucency with thick wall; a cavity >1 cm is significant
Defines wall thickness, air‑fluid level, and surrounding consolidation; useful when X‑ray is equivocal

sections.p: Cavities reflect advanced disease and high bacillary load. They are associated with poor treatment response and higher relapse rates. In low‑resource settings, sputum smear, GeneXpert and basic imaging are the mainstays.

t.b: Detects acid‑fast bacilli; a positive result in a cavity patient confirms infectiousness
Rapid detection of MTB DNA and rifampicin resistance; essential when drug resistance is suspected

b: Haemoptysis >30 ml/day is a red flag
sections.p: Patients present with chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and haemoptysis. In HIV‑co‑infected patients, cavities may be atypical or absent. Early recognition prevents transmission and guides surgical consideration.

t.b: Positive in most TB patients; a negative test does not exclude cavity disease in high‑risk groups
Dullness over cavity; bronchial breath sounds may be heard if air‑fluid level

b: Ask about prior TB treatment – relapse risk
sections.p: Examine the patient’s history for TB exposure, HIV status and previous treatment. On exam, look for signs of chronic disease and assess for haemoptysis. Radiology is the cornerstone; sputum tests confirm the diagnosis.

t.b: Gold standard for drug susceptibility; takes 6–8 weeks but essential for guiding therapy

b: Do not rely solely on X‑ray; confirm with sputum
sections.p: Assuming all cavitary lesions are TB; overlooking fungal or bacterial abscesses. Misinterpreting a thin‑walled cavity as benign. Ignoring haemoptysis as a surgical emergency.

t.b: Useful when sputum is negative but cavity suspected; can obtain lavage for culture

whenToSeekHelp: Severe haemoptysis (>30 ml/day), sudden respiratory distress, or signs of septic shock
